UNDERSTANDING IN VISIONS AND DREAMS
“Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams.”
Daniel 1:17 (KJV) →
HOW THE WORD KEPT COMING
“The secret” of the king's dream was “revealed unto Daniel in a night vision”, after he and his companions asked mercy of “the God of heaven”; Daniel then blessed God for it. Daniel 2:17–23
He interpreted what others saw: the king's dream of the image, the king's dream of the tree, and the writing on the wall. Daniel 2:36–45 Daniel 4:19–27 Daniel 5:25–28
Later he had dreams and visions of his own, and wrote them down: “he wrote the dream, and told the sum of the matters.” Daniel 7:1 Daniel 7:15–16

Gabriel is named twice as the one who makes him understand. In the last vision “a certain man clothed in linen” appears, and “one like the similitude of the sons of men” touches his lips. Daniel 8:16 Daniel 9:21–22 Daniel 10:5–6 Daniel 10:16

In Darius's first year he “understood by books” the seventy years of Jerusalem's desolation that the word of the LORD gave to Jeremiah, and prayed “with fasting, and sackcloth, and ashes”. Daniel 9:2–3
Before his last vision he mourned three full weeks, eating “no pleasant bread”. Daniel 10:2–3

From the textThe book never says that the word of the LORD came to Daniel, and it never calls Daniel a prophet; it uses “prophet” only of Jeremiah and of “thy servants the prophets”. Daniel 9:2 Daniel 9:6 Daniel 9:10
Jesus speaks of “the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet” (Matthew 24:15; the King James text of Mark 13:14 has the same words). Matthew 24:15 Mark 13:14
At Daniel 2:4 the Chaldeans answer the king “in Syriack”. Daniel 2:4

Scholars' viewDriver (1891) notes that the book is written “partly in Hebrew, partly in Aramaic”, the Aramaic running from the words “O king” in 2:4 to the end of chapter 7. Daniel 2:4 Daniel 7:28 [1]

HOW THE STORY ENDS
Scripture says, tradition says
SCRIPTURE SAYS
Daniel 1 closes with “And Daniel continued even unto the first year of king Cyrus.” His last dated vision is “in the third year of Cyrus king of Persia”. Daniel 1:21 Daniel 10:1
The last words to him are a promise: “go thou thy way till the end be: for thou shalt rest, and stand in thy lot at the end of the days.” Daniel 12:13
TRADITION SAYS

Benjamin of Tudela, who travelled between 1165 and 1173, describes “the sepulchre of Daniel” at Shushan, and tells how its coffin was moved from one bank of the river to the other until the Persian ruler Sinjar had it set in a coffin of crystal and hung from the middle of the bridge.[29] Who says so: Benjamin of Tudela, Itinerary (tr. Adler 1907), 1165–1173
OPEN QUESTIONS
Where readers have differed
By Daniel, in the sixth century BC
E. B. Pusey (1864); C. F. Keil (1872); R. Dick Wilson in ISBE (1915)

Keil holds that the testimony of synagogue and church to the book's “composition by the prophet Daniel, rests on a solid foundation”, and that in antiquity only the Neo-Platonist Porphyry doubted it. Pusey calls the book “either Divine or an imposture”, and lists among his proofs that the “Testimony of our Lord stands alone, as infallible”. Wilson answers the arguments from the Greek names of instruments and the Persian words, holding that a sixth-century writer “may have known and used borrowed Greek terms”. Matthew 24:15 [15][6][27]
In its present form, in the time of Antiochus Epiphanes, on a basis of tradition
S. R. Driver (1891)

Driver argues from the book's place among the Writings rather than the Prophets, the silence of Ben Sira, the Persian and Greek words, and the theology, that it was “not written earlier than c. 300 B.C.”, and that grounds exist which, “though not adequate to demonstrate”, yet “make the opinion a probable one, that the Book, as we have it, is a work of the age of Antiochus Epiphanes”. He adds: “Daniel, it cannot be doubted, was a historical person”.[1]
The stories (1–6) from the third century BC, the visions (7–12) from 168–165 BC
J. A. Montgomery (1927)

Montgomery assigns chapters 1–6 to Babylonia, “roughly … to the 3d cent.”, as a collection of stories “based on Jewish and Bab. traditions”, and holds that chapters 7–12 “belong to the first years of the Macc. uprising, 168-165 B.C.”[11]

WHAT SCRIPTURE DOES NOT SAY
Daniel's book does not name his father, his tribe or his age; it says only that he was among “the children of Judah” chosen from the captives (Dan 1:3–6).
Daniel is not mentioned in the story of the golden image and the furnace (Dan 3); the book does not say where he was.
The book never calls Daniel a prophet; the title is Jesus' (Matt 24:15).
Daniel does not name the second, third or fourth kingdoms of chapters 2 and 7; only chapter 8 names Media and Persia and Grecia.
Who Darius the Mede was is not explained in Daniel; the views are on his ruler page.
Scripture does not say where or when Daniel died.
